course_description: This course traces the gendered development of contemporary cultures. Popular media represents a form of cultural power that is produced by and reflected in gendered ideals, as seen through the written word, broadcasts, and digital worlds. Students will interrogate how gender and identity are rendered significant through popular culture, critically engaging with questions of power, privilege, and inequalities. Using gender and sexuality frameworks, with an intersectional focus on decolonial scholarship, queer theory, and critical disability studies, this course situates everyday cultural sites at the centre of meaningful inquiry in the Humanities.

course_aims: This course aims to ground the theoretical study of gender in the very tangible outputs of popular culture and media. This subject explores key sites of contemporary culture through which gender identities develop, transform, and dominate. The use of feminist, queer, trans, decolonial, and critical disability studies will inform how we approach media in this course, across multiple national contexts. Students will learn to critically engage with debates around producers and consumers, and to assess contemporaneous impact and reception over time. Broadly focusing on three areas—text, broadcast, and digital—we will examine how gender is central to the production of cultural artefacts, and how these artefacts in turn influence the ways gender is constructed in the ‘real’ world.

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse key sites through which gender identities emerge.
Examine media representations of bodies, genders and sexualities through intersectional gendered theoretical frameworks.
An interdisciplinary approach to media analysis.
Research evidence and articulate arguments about culture, media, and gender.
The ability to think critically and analytically about gender representation in the world around them, and to articulate those thoughts in writing.

assessment_details.title: Tutorial Participation
assessment_details.task_description: Tutorials commence in Week 2 of semester. The participation mark will be determined by considering a student’s overall participation in the tutorial series. The quality of a student’s contribution (not mere frequency of attendance) will be the main criteria. To ensure you do well in tutorials you should always: Do the readings. Think about the broader implications of the topic in terms of theory and real-world applications. Contribute to discussions meaningfully. Engage respectfully with others. assessment_details.title: Video Essay Proposal
assessment_details.task_description: You will provide a research proposal outlining your intended approach to your Video Essay. You may choose any aspect of gender and contemporary culture to focus on. This proposal will include a research question/s, argument, and main points you intend to use to support your argument and answer your research question. You will also provide an annotated bibliography of at least 5 scholarly sources you will use in your Video Essay, providing analysis of the sources in relation to your chosen topic. More information on this will be made available in lectures and/or tutorials. Referencing Syle: Students may choose whichever referencing style they are comfortable with, as long as it remains consistent with the UQ Library style guide: https://guides.library.uq.edu.au/referencing. All referencing requires specific page numbers. Word Limits: A final word count that is within ±10% of the set length (500 words) is acceptable. Word count does not include any referencing or bibliography; however, discursive footnotes are included in the word count. A word count that is outside these 10% will receive a proportionate penalty and will be graded against the grading criteria. AI: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools.
